title: Nia and the Sleepy Bee
markdown:
The moon, a pale soft disc in the dark quiet sky, was just beginning its journey, painting the world in gentle silver light. Nia the nightjar, nestled deep within the warm hollow of an old oak tree, blinked her large kind eyes. Her feathers, soft as the last whisper of twilight, were already settling for the night. But Nia’s always-listening ears caught a faint busy buzzing. It was her friend, Pollen the bee, still flitting amongst the blossoms, tiny wings a soft blur against the moonlit petals. Nia noticed how Pollen’s flight seemed a little slower, a little more tired than usual, and a small worry fluttered in her feathery chest.

Gently, so as not to startle the busy bee, Nia called out in her low soft voice, “Pollen, little friend, why are you still working so hard? The moon is high, and the world is whispering sleep now.” Her voice was like the softest rustle of leaves, a gentle invitation to rest.

Pollen paused, little antennae twitching, and hovered near Nia’s hollow. “Oh, Nia,” she buzzed, her voice a little weary, like a tiny sigh. “I have so many more flowers to visit. There is still so much nectar to gather before the morning arrives.” She pictured her hive, imagining every single drop of golden honey. Her little bee heart felt a need to hurry.

Nia tilted her head, gaze full of warm concern. “But Pollen, your wings are moving so slowly now. If you don’t rest, you’ll be too tired for all the wonderful flowers tomorrow. The night is for slumber, for dreams to bloom in your mind.” Nia herself felt a delightful heaviness in her own little birdy bones, a sure sign it was time to nestle down. She imagined how the soft moonlight would feel like a warm blanket, and the gentle breeze would sing a lullaby just for her. “When you sleep, your little wings get strong again, and your tiny bee-brain can think of all the best flowers for the new day.”

Pollen landed on a soft leaf, tiny legs wiggling as she tried to stand steady. “I worry, Nia,” she confessed, her voice barely a buzz. “What if all the sweetest nectar is gone by the time the sun wakes? What if I miss out on the very best gifts the flowers have to offer?” She imagined her hive without enough precious honey, and the thought made her tiny fuzzy body feel a little droopy.

Nia ruffled her soft feathers, a comforting movement. “Ah, but here’s the curious thing about flowers, little Pollen,” she murmured, her voice a gentle lullaby weaving through the quiet air. “They are so kind. They bloom anew with every sunrise, offering their sweetness with joy. They know you will need them, and they will always be waiting. You just need to trust them to rest until then.” Nia remembered her own cozy hollow, how safe and warm it felt, and the wonderful clear dreams that came when she truly let herself sleep. “Think of the energy you’ll have to explore the dew-kissed meadows tomorrow.”

Pollen looked around. The moonbeams were like soft blankets falling on the meadow, touching each blade of grass with silver. The night air was cool and smelled of sweet clover and dew, a gentle perfume that made her feel peaceful. A deep tiredness settled over her, like a warm hug. Her wings, which had worked so hard all day, felt heavy indeed, like tiny little weights. She heard the gentle hum of the night, felt the soft clover beneath her legs, and smelled the sweet cool air. She saw Nia’s calm understanding eyes, and they were like twin moons reflecting kindness.

“You are right, Nia,” Pollen whispered, her buzz now very soft, like the hum of a contented dream. “My wings are tired. And I do want to dream of flowers.” With a final happy little buzz, a sound of sweet surrender, she settled onto a patch of dew-kissed clover, its tiny petals curling slightly around her, making a perfect soft bed. Nia watched as Pollen tucked her little legs beneath her and closed her tiny bee eyes. The moonlight seemed to cradle her, making her golden stripes glow softly, a tiny beacon of peaceful slumber.

Nia blinked once more, then tucked her own twilight feathers close. The oak hollow held two kinds of quiet now: a bird’s, and a bee’s. Tomorrow the flowers would wait. Tonight they did not have to.
